summary: Italy's military said Friday that its navy had recovered the fishing boat Airone hours after armed men seized it. Naval personnel boarded the vessel about 90 kilometers (56 miles) from Libya's port of Misrata and detained a Libyan soldier, according to Italian military statements. The navy said accidental rifle fire during the operation slightly wounded one of the seven fishermen aboard. The crew, comprising three Sicilians and four Tunisians, had left Sicily five days earlier to catch shrimp.

Novak Djokovic extended his current winning streak to 17 matches after beating Thomas Berdych 7-5, 4-6, 6-3 in the rain-interrupted final of the Monte Carlo Masters. "It was a tough match, a particular match," said Djokovic after winning his 52nd career title, and his second Monte Carlo Masters championship. After winning the Australian Open back in January, Djokovic has followed up with Masters' victories at Indian Wells and Miami. Sunday's victory over Berdych means he becomes the first man to win the opening three Masters tournaments of the season.

Former Satyam Computers Services chairman Ramalinga Raju and nine others received seven-year prison sentences after convictions for offenses including cheating, conspiracy and breach of public trust, Indian authorities said. Raju also received an $804,000 fine, according to a Central Bureau of Investigation spokesman. The $1.6 billion fraud case emerged in 2009 when Raju acknowledged fabricating assets and cash to inflate profits, while investigators said investors' losses were considerably larger. Following his disclosures, the government dismissed Satyam's board, and Tech Mahindra purchased the company through a state-backed auction.

Johan Bavman is documenting the real-life experience of fathers taking full advantage of Sweden's 480 calendar days of parental leave, capturing their devotion and tiredness in realistic imagery. Bavman says only 12% of Swedish couples equally share the leave, and he is looking for a total of 60 fathers to photograph for an exhibition and a book.

Officials said ISIS freed more than 200 Yazidis in northern Iraq on Wednesday, mostly women and children, with the remainder elderly or ill. Kurdish forces received the former captives and sent them to Irbil, but the reason for their release remained unknown.

Philadelphia police added an attempted-murder charge against Nyia Parler, accused of abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in a park for more than four days while visiting her boyfriend in Maryland. Parler was arrested in Maryland, but police said she must finish unspecified treatment before she can be extradited to Philadelphia.

New research released by the Anne Frank House concludes that Anne and her older sister, Margot Frank, probably did not survive to March 1945, dying at least a month earlier than previously thought. Witnesses at the camp said both sisters had symptoms of typhus before February 7, but the exact dates of death remain unclear.

Bundchen walked the runway for the last time Wednesday, and the New England Patriots quarterback wasn't just there to support her in person, he expressed his emotions to the world on Facebook. "I want to be with my family more and focus on special projects," she said.

French police said investigators had finished gathering the principal evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site and were not expected to return. The aircraft crashed in the Alps on March 24, killing all 150 people aboard. Recovery teams found the flight data recorder Thursday, after recovering the cockpit voice recorder days after the crash. Prosecutor Brice Robin said laboratories had identified 150 DNA profiles from more than 2,000 samples collected at the site. Authorities say co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately crashed the plane after preventing the captain from reentering the cockpit, and France's BEA said preliminary recorder analysis showed he intentionally accelerated its descent. Lubitz had previously experienced depression and withheld recent medical notes declaring him unfit to work from his employer. A private security company will protect the site until the remaining wreckage is removed to secure locations for any further examination.

With his early leap into the 2016 race, Marco Rubio is positioning himself as the next generation of GOP leadership. The Republican senator from Florida has announced that he is seeking the Republican presidential nomination, running on an optimistic message that he embodies the promise of the American Dream. Yet Rubio has been his own worst enemy on what could have been his two signature issues: immigration reform and Cuba relations. Back in 2013, Rubio was a member of the Senate "Gang of 8" that crafted a bipartisan proposal for comprehensive reform, including a path to citizenship for the nation's estimated 11 million undocumented immigrants. He later distanced himself from the bill after it ran into resistance from House Republicans, and now says he favors a piecemeal approach, starting with securing the border. No wonder the research firm Latino Decisions reports that, "We find no evidence that Rubio's candidacy will draw significant Latino support for his candidacy or for his party more generally." Most Americans support better relations with Cuba, as do a majority of Cuban-Americans. By clinging to the notion that isolating Cuba is better than engaging with the communist country, Rubio has marginalized himself on an issue where he could have provided insight and leadership. Another Rubio weakness is his lack of bold policy proposals. Unfortunately, a fresh face on stale ideas is not a winning combination -- not for Rubio, and not for Latino voters.

Sudan's female companions, Fatu and Najin, live at the conservancy, where experts are scrambling to ensure the subspecies does not go extinct. He's the last known male northern white rhino left in the entire world. A total of five remain in captivity worldwide: three in Kenya, and one each at zoos in San Diego and the Czech Republic. A committee at the conservancy is also looking at various alternative reproduction techniques, including in vitro fertilization.

President Obama and his Cuban counterpart, Raul Castro, greeted each other and shook hands Friday night at a dinner in Panama City for the Summit of the Americas, after a half-century of enmity between their nations. They were expected to spend more time together Saturday, with their interactions representing the highest-level talks between the United States and Cuba since Richard Nixon and Fidel Castro met in 1959. Obama is seeking to engage Havana in talks over reopening embassies and removing barriers to commerce and travel as part of the ongoing process of normalizing relations. In Panama, Obama is expected to announce he is removing Cuba from the United States' list of countries that sponsor terrorism, but a panel of experts was reviewing the State Department's report before his final determination.

Jamal al-Labani had hoped to bring his pregnant wife and young daughter back to the United States from war-torn Yemen, but family members identified him as a victim killed in a mortar strike last week in Aden. The 45-year-old was on his way back from mosque prayers Tuesday evening when he was hit in the back by shrapnel from a mortar shell and died minutes later, his family said. He is believed to be the first U.S. citizen killed in the current violence in Yemen. For the past three weeks, al-Labani had told family members he was concerned about not being able to evacuate as the situation deteriorated, according to his cousin Mohammed Alazzani. More than 200 people have been killed in Aden in the past 11 days, according to Naef Al Bakri, Aden's deputy governor. Violence is intensifying as Saudi Arabia and other Arab nations target Houthi rebels in Yemen with airstrikes. Yemeni-Americans are trapped in the conflict but haven't gotten enough help from the U.S. government, the Council on American-Islamic Relations told CNN. Responding to the criticism, the U.S. State Department said there are no current plans to evacuate private U.S. citizens from Yemen and encouraged them to shelter in a secure location until they can depart safely using available commercial transportation. The International Committee of the Red Cross said Sunday that Saudi Arabia has signed off on the delivery of medical supplies and personnel to Yemen, where time was running out to save those wounded in airstrikes and ground fighting.

Law enforcement officials said Saturday that the FBI was examining a potential terrorist threat in the United States that might have been inspired by ISIS. Intercepted communications and other intelligence prompted concern that someone could be planning an attack. No one had been arrested, and officials had not established whether the threat reflected an actual plan or merely an aspiration. Its precise nature was unknown, although an official said the inquiry concerned parts of California where security had been strengthened. The TSA notified police responsible for security outside airports, but officials cautioned that the possible threat did not necessarily involve aviation. Several American cities increased precautions, while a Homeland Security spokesman declined to discuss this case and instead described broader measures introduced in recent months. Those measures included stronger screening at selected overseas airports, more random passenger and baggage searches on flights to the United States, additional travel-authorization safeguards and a greater police presence at federal facilities.

Lewis Hamilton took victory for Mercedes at the Chinese Grand Prix, capturing his 35th grand prix win with a pole-to-flag win in Shanghai. Nico Rosberg came home second for Mercedes, while Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel finished third to collect his third straight podium of 2015. Vettel is just 13 points behind Hamilton in the world championship and four points ahead of Rosberg, after the first three races of the year. Rosberg complained after the race that Hamilton's slow driving was holding him up, bringing Vettel closer and taking life out of his tyres. Hamilton said he didn't do anything intentionally to slow the cars down and that Rosberg could have tried to get by, but didn't. Hamilton has won two grands prix in 2015 while Rosberg has yet to climb onto the top step of the podium. Rosberg has another chance at the Bahrain Grand Prix in seven days, where Ferrari will hope the hot track temperatures help them topple Mercedes again.

Universal's "Furious 7" continues to build momentum at the Friday box office for a weekend debut in the $135 million-$138 million range, the largest opening in North America since fall 2013. The final film featuring the late Paul Walker, "Furious 7" is opening around the globe this weekend and earned a record-breaking $60 million internationally on Wednesday and Thursday for a possible worldwide debut approaching or crossing $300 million by the end of Easter Sunday.

Delaware father Steve Esmond is in stable condition and improving as his two teenage sons remain in critical condition after the family became sick -- perhaps from pesticide exposure, federal officials say -- during a trip to the U.S. Virgin Islands. The teens' mother, Theresa Devine, was treated at a hospital and released, and is in occupational therapy, according to the family's attorney, James Maron. An EPA spokesman said preliminary test results showed the presence of methyl bromide in the family's rented villa at the Sirenusa resort in St. John; the pesticide is not allowed to be used indoors. The EPA is investigating whether a March 18 fumigation at the resort caused the illnesses and whether environmental regulations or laws were violated, while the U.S. Department of Justice has initiated a criminal investigation.

While the fight against ISIS in Syria and Iraq holds the world's gaze, a simultaneous transformation is getting less attention: the deterioration of al Qaeda. In an audio message released Sunday, al Qaeda confirmed that two of its leaders, known as Ustad Ahmad Farooq and Qari Abdullah Mansur, were killed in CIA drone strikes in January in North Waziristan, near the Afghan-Pakistan border. Farooq's real name was Raja Mohammad Suleman, al Qaeda said. (Mansur's real name was Qari Ubaidullah, a Pakistani who oversaw suicide missions against U.S. and NATO troops in Afghanistan). The deaths of Ubaidullah and Suleman underline the fact that there are almost no top leaders of al Qaeda left except al-Zawahiri. Indeed, al Qaeda has virtually no capacity to carry out attacks in the West. To be sure, al Qaeda's Yemen-based affiliate, al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, continues to pose a threat to American aviation. The group also trained one of the gunmen who attacked the offices of the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo in Paris in January, killing 12, but it's not clear if AQAP had any direct role in planning this attack. Meanwhile, ISIS continues to attract Western recruits and also inspire "homegrown" terrorists in the West, but the core al Qaeda organization that killed almost 3,000 men, women and children on 9/11 is on life support.
